scenarioSubtitle: Designing an AI-enabled SME banking journey for Aisha
description: You have just interviewed Aisha — a restaurant owner and SME banking customer. You know her problems: cash flow uncertainty, working capital pressure, FX costs on supplier invoices, and a bank that has never treated her as anything more than a transaction. Now you design the AI decisions that will shape her journey. Seven stages. Three choices each. The right answer is rarely the most obvious one.

rounds.title: How much AI should the bank spend reaching Aisha — when it doesn't know her value yet?
rounds.tradeoffTagline: 💸 Inference cost vs 🎯 Acquisition quality — the CLV certainty problem
rounds.prompt: Aisha has run her restaurant for six years. She's outgrown her current bank — no relationship, no intelligence, no real support for a growing SME. Last week she saw outreach from three banks. She opened one of them. The bank must decide how much AI inference to invest in reaching SME prospects whose lifetime value is still entirely unknown. Overspend here and the budget is unavailable at Engagement and Expansion — where Aisha's value is proven and AI investment generates 4–8x the return.

options.label: Run a frontier LLM to generate a fully personalised message for every SME prospect — Aisha's restaurant name, her sector, her growth stage, individually generated. Every prospect receives the same level of model inference regardless of conversion likelihood. Cost: £1.2M. Cost per prospect: £0.08.
options.insightExperience: Aisha received a message that named her restaurant and referenced her sector. She opened it. So did 14,999 other SMEs — each with individually generated content, regardless of whether the bank had any signal they would convert or stay.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £0.08 per prospect, the bank spent £1.2M on acquisition inference — at the stage of lowest CLV certainty in the entire simulation. The frontier model budget consumed here is unavailable at Engagement, where a CFO agent catching Aisha's cash flow crisis in October generates £3.5M in retained lifetime value. The three-layer framework is explicit: match inference investment to CLV certainty. At acquisition, certainty is zero.
options.insightRevenue: The bank acquired customers — but spent £800K more than Option B to do it. That £800K compounds negatively: it is not available to invest in the engagement and expansion stages where proven CLV justifies frontier model spend. Revenue trail runs below the optimal path from Engagement onward.

compareSummary.reason: Reaches Aisha but at three times the cost per prospect, with no CLV signal to justify frontier inference. The quality of the acquired customer is not better — just the quality of the message.

options.explanation: Running frontier inference per prospect mistakes AI effort for AI value. At acquisition, the bank has no reliable CLV signal for any individual prospect. The cost per inference (£0.08) produces a marginally better message than a well-crafted sector template (£0.02) — but the revenue consequence of that margin is negligible. What is not negligible: £800K spent here is £800K unavailable when Aisha faces a real cash flow crisis at Engagement and a CFO agent catching it is worth £3.5M in retained lifetime value. Experience decision: Aisha needs to feel the bank understands her world — not that it knows her name. Architecture decision: template automation, not frontier inference. Commercial decision: the inference cost of £0.08 per prospect cannot be recovered from acquisition conversion rates alone. The right model runs where value is certain.

options.label: Cluster SMEs into eight sector archetypes — restaurant owners, independent retailers, tech startups, professional services — and build human-reviewed outreach for each type. The LLM drafts and refines the templates; simple automation delivers at scale. Aisha receives a message that speaks her world without per-prospect inference. Cost: £400K. Cost per prospect: £0.02.
options.insightExperience: Aisha received a message that read: 'We work with growing restaurant businesses across London — here's how we support businesses at your stage.' It didn't name her restaurant. It understood her world. She opened it. The bank spent £400K instead of £1.2M.
options.insightCostDrivers: Template personalisation at £0.02 per prospect achieves 85% of the conversion impact of frontier inference at 25% of the cost. At acquisition — where every prospect's CLV is unknown — the marginal experience value of individually generated AI content does not justify a 4x cost premium. The £800K saved is available for the Engagement stage, where the same budget funds a CFO agent that prevents Aisha from churning during a cash flow crisis.
options.insightRevenue: Better-matched customers from budget-disciplined acquisition enter the journey with appropriate expectations. The compounding effect is structural: every pound not spent on frontier inference at acquisition can be deployed where AI generates 4–8x the return on proven CLV. The revenue advantage builds from Engagement onward.

compareSummary.reason: Achieves equivalent acquisition quality at one-third the cost, preserving £800K for the stages where CLV is proven and inference investment pays back at the highest rate.

options.explanation: This is the correct decision — and the one that requires understanding the first principle of AI economics: match inference investment to CLV certainty. At acquisition, certainty is zero. The experience decision: Aisha needs to feel the bank understands her world, not that it can generate a message with her name in it. A well-crafted sector archetype template — 'growing restaurant businesses in London' — achieves this. The architecture decision: the LLM is used to draft and refine eight excellent templates, not to run inference at scale across 15,000 prospects. The commercial decision: £0.02 per prospect, total £400K, £800K preserved for Engagement. At Engagement, that £800K funds a CFO agent that catches Aisha's cash flow problem in October before she knows it exists — and that intervention is worth £3.5M in retained lifetime value. The right model for the right moment.

options.label: Train an ML model on the bank's existing SME transaction data to score every prospect by predicted conversion likelihood. Direct AI-personalised outreach to the top 20%. Aisha — artisan restaurant, niche cuisine, atypical financial profile — is ranked middle tier and receives a standard campaign. Cost: £600K.
options.insightExperience: Aisha received a standard campaign. The scoring model ranked her as a moderate-probability prospect — her artisan Middle Eastern restaurant concept, niche cuisine, and unconventional cash flow patterns didn't match the profiles in the training data, which was built on the bank's existing SME base.
options.insightCostDrivers: The scoring model cost £600K to build and deploy — £200K more than Option B, with worse acquisition outcomes. The deeper cost is structural: a model trained on existing customers systematically learns to identify businesses that look like the bank's current base. Aisha — and businesses like her — represent the highest-upside growth opportunity precisely because they are underserved by conventional banks. The model excluded them.
options.insightRevenue: The bank reached the prospects it already knew. Atypical SMEs — often the highest-growth segment — were systematically deprioritised. The customer base entering the journey skews toward conventional archetypes. The innovation and growth in the bank's SME portfolio is suppressed from stage one.

compareSummary.reason: Costs £200K more than Option B with weaker outcomes — and the scoring model's training bias systematically excludes the highest-potential, most underserved SME segment.

options.explanation: Lead scoring sounds like the most sophisticated approach. It isn't — not without addressing the model's training bias. The ML model was trained on the bank's existing customers: businesses it has already acquired, already served, and already selected through previous acquisition campaigns. It has learned to identify prospects that look like those businesses. Aisha's artisan restaurant — niche cuisine, unconventional seasonality, atypical working capital patterns — doesn't match. The model ranks her as moderate-probability. She receives a standard campaign. She opens an account elsewhere. The systematic exclusion of atypical, high-upside SMEs compounds: the bank's portfolio becomes progressively more conventional, more commoditised, and more exposed to competitors who build acquisition models that seek out the underserved segment instead of replicating the existing one.

rounds.title: Aisha's application flags an anomaly. What does the bank's AI do next?
rounds.tradeoffTagline: ⚡ Speed and automation vs 🤝 Trust formation vs 💰 Unit economics
rounds.prompt: Aisha has applied. Her business structure is more complex than a standard SME: she has a personal account, a trading account for the restaurant, and a second entity registered for a catering operation she runs on the side. The automated identity checks flag an anomaly — a mismatch between the two entities. This is the most formative moment in the relationship. The bank must decide how its AI handles the next thirty minutes of Aisha's experience.

options.label: The AI processes Aisha's application automatically — identity verified, anomaly resolved algorithmically, account configured. Aisha receives no explanation of what was flagged or how it was resolved. Completion time: 4 minutes. Cost: £800K. Cost per onboarding: £57.
options.insightExperience: Aisha's application completed in 4 minutes. Two weeks later, a payment instruction was automatically queried. She didn't know why — the same system that processed her onboarding silently was now silently querying her transactions. She called support twice in the first month.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £57 per onboarding, this is cheaper than Option C by £21 per customer. Across 14,000 annual SME onboardings, the saving is £294K. The compounding cost of the trust deficit — lower activation, lower feature adoption, higher support contact rate — exceeds that saving by Engagement. The cost-per-interaction metric looked good. The unit economics of the relationship deteriorated.
options.insightRevenue: Trust destroyed at onboarding does not recover. The AIX Trust dimension — the experience must be reliable, explainable, and safe — is violated at the most formative stage of the relationship. Lower adoption, weaker engagement, and a support cost spike compound through every stage that follows.

compareSummary.reason: Saves £21 per customer at onboarding, then loses it back in higher support costs, lower activation rates, and weaker lifetime value — the trust deficit is the most expensive outcome in the simulation.

options.explanation: Speed without explainability is the core failure at this stage. The AI resolves the anomaly correctly — but Aisha never knows what was flagged, what decision was made, or on what basis. At the moment she forms her first real impression of the bank's intelligence, the experience is opaque. The AIX framework is explicit on this: Trust requires the experience to be reliable, explainable, and safe — especially for high-stakes financial decisions. Agency & Control requires that the customer understands what the AI is doing and why. Full automation without transparency violates both dimensions at the moment they matter most. The cost saving of £21 per customer at onboarding is real. The cost of the trust deficit that follows — in higher support contact rates, lower feature activation, weaker engagement depth, and reduced resilience to competitive pressure at Retention — is not.

options.label: The bank assigns a dedicated SME relationship specialist to Aisha's onboarding. The specialist manages the full process — AI-assisted but human-led. Aisha has one named contact, full transparency, and an advocate inside the bank from day one. Cost: £2.2M. Cost per onboarding: £157.
options.insightExperience: Aisha's onboarding was exceptional. Her relationship specialist called within 20 minutes, explained the entity mismatch clearly, resolved it in a single conversation, and followed up to confirm everything was configured correctly. She told her accountant the bank was different.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £157 per onboarding — compared to £78 for Option C — the premium is real. Across 14,000 annual SME onboardings, the additional cost versus Option C is £1.1M per year. The experience quality is high. The question is whether the bank can deploy a dedicated specialist to 14,000 customers annually and still sustain the unit economics of the SME segment. The answer, at scale, is no — and the budget consumed here reduces what is available for Engagement and Expansion, where proven CLV justifies investment.
options.insightRevenue: Excellent early trust — but the model does not scale. By Expansion, the budget drain from an unsustainable onboarding model has reduced the bank's capacity to invest in the AI intelligence that drives Aisha's most valuable moment: the decision to open her second restaurant.

compareSummary.reason: Creates the best initial trust — but at a per-customer cost that breaks the unit economics of the SME segment at scale, and consumes budget that should be reserved for Engagement and Expansion.

options.explanation: The experience quality is not in question — a dedicated relationship specialist creates the highest trust outcome at onboarding. The economics are. The bank serves 14,000 SME customers annually. A dedicated specialist for each costs £157 per onboarding, or £2.2M per year in onboarding cost alone. That is £1.1M more than Option C — and £1.1M unavailable for the CFO agent at Engagement that prevents cash flow crises, or the expansion recommendation system that helps Aisha evaluate Hackney. The three-layer framework is explicit: the architecture decision must sustain margin, not just maximise experience at individual touchpoints. A premium concierge model is the right answer for a private bank serving 500 high-net-worth clients. It is the wrong answer for a digital SME bank trying to serve 50,000 customers with positive unit economics.

options.label: The AI walks Aisha through each step of onboarding, explains what it is doing and why, flags the entity anomaly to a human reviewer who contacts her within 30 minutes, and confirms with Aisha what was found and resolved. Aisha stays informed throughout. Cost: £1.1M. Cost per onboarding: £78.
options.insightExperience: Aisha was guided through each step. When her entity documentation triggered a review, the system explained what had been flagged and routed the case to a human reviewer. The reviewer called within 25 minutes and resolved the issue transparently. Aisha knew what happened and why. That transparency — at the most formative moment — became the foundation of the relationship.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £78 per onboarding, this is £21 more per customer than full automation and £79 less than the dedicated specialist model. The AI handles the explainability and routing; humans handle the exception. The marginal cost of the human review step is what produces the trust outcome. The AI does not replace the human at the high-stakes moment — it identifies when the human is needed and routes efficiently.
options.insightRevenue: Trust built at onboarding compounds through every stage that follows. Customers who understand what the bank's AI did — and why — adopt more services, engage more deeply, and are significantly more resilient to competitive pressure at Retention and Loyalty. This is the highest single-stage leverage point in the simulation.

compareSummary.reason: At £79 less per customer than the specialist model, it delivers comparable trust outcomes through intelligent design — explainability built into the AI, human escalation for genuine exceptions — and preserves budget for Engagement and Expansion.

options.explanation: This is the correct decision — and the one that embeds all four AIX dimensions correctly at the most formative stage of the relationship. Contextual Specificity: the AI understands Aisha's business structure is complex and adapts. Intent Alignment: the system is optimised for Aisha's outcome (completing onboarding with confidence) not the bank's operational efficiency metric. Trust: every decision is explained, every exception is escalated to a human, Aisha knows what happened and why. Agency & Control: Aisha remains informed throughout — the AI acts within visible, understandable boundaries. At £78 per onboarding, the model is scalable: the AI handles the majority of the journey; human expertise is deployed only where it changes the outcome. The cost difference versus full automation is £21 per customer. The trust difference is the entire subsequent trajectory of the relationship.

rounds.title: Aisha needs to configure payroll, EUR supplier payments, and cash alerts. When should the AI intervene?
rounds.tradeoffTagline: ⏱️ Inference timing vs 📊 Guidance relevance — the context-trigger problem
rounds.prompt: Aisha has opened her account. She needs to configure three things: payroll for her 12 employees, a recurring payment schedule for her two main food suppliers (both invoicing in euros), and automatic cash flow alerts tied to her payroll dates. She has never set up these features with a bank before. The bank must decide when and how its AI provides guidance — and how much that inference costs per interaction.

options.label: The AI generates contextual guidance based on what Aisha is actually doing — then caches it and updates only when her behaviour signals a genuine context change. She gets a payroll walkthrough when she starts the payroll setup, an FX alert explanation when she initiates her first euro payment. Silent when nothing has changed. Cost: £700K. Cost per interaction: £0.04.
options.insightExperience: Aisha set up payroll with a step-by-step walkthrough that appeared precisely when she started the process. When she initiated her first euro supplier payment, the AI surfaced an explanation of the bank's FX rate and alternatives — exactly when she needed it. Between those moments, the system was quiet. The guidance felt earned, not intrusive.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £0.04 per interaction, the behavioral trigger model runs inference only when Aisha's actions signal a new context — a new feature, a new transaction type, a behaviour change. Between triggers, cached guidance is served. The result: AI runs at 35% of the frequency of a session-by-session model, at 40% of the cost, with no perceptible quality loss for the customer. The budget saved is available for the CFO agent at Engagement.
options.insightRevenue: Customers who activate the right features — payroll, FX, alerts — in their first month generate measurably higher engagement depth and lifetime value. The activation-retention linkage is explicit in the CEI model: strong activation produces approximately 7x higher retention probability (Amplitude, 2024). Guidance that arrives at the right moment drives completion; guidance that arrives on a schedule often arrives at the wrong moment.

compareSummary.reason: Delivers the same contextual intelligence as Option B at 44% of the cost — the inference trigger is customer behaviour, not session start. AI runs when the context has changed, not on a fixed schedule.

options.explanation: This is the correct decision — and it requires understanding the most important cost architecture principle in LLM systems: inference frequency drives cost more than model quality. A session-by-session model runs inference 140,000 times per year across the SME activation base. A behaviour-triggered model runs inference when a customer does something genuinely new — approximately 49,000 times. Same model. Same quality. 35% of the inference cost. The guidance Aisha receives is contextually specific (she gets payroll help when she's doing payroll, FX guidance when she's doing FX), intentionally aligned to what she's trying to accomplish at that moment, trustworthy because it's relevant, and agency-preserving because it doesn't overwhelm her with unsolicited prompts. The £900K saved versus Option B is available for the Engagement stage — where Aisha will need a CFO agent to catch a cash flow problem she doesn't yet know is coming.

options.label: Run the bank's highest-capability reasoning model at every session — fresh inference every time Aisha opens the app, regardless of whether anything has changed in her account or her behaviour. Maximum guidance quality at every touchpoint. Cost: £1.6M. Cost per interaction: £0.11.
options.insightExperience: Aisha received high-quality guidance every time she opened the app — including on visits where she simply checked her balance or reviewed a transaction. The guidance was excellent. It was also often irrelevant to what she was actually doing. After two weeks, she started dismissing the prompts without reading them.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £0.11 per interaction and 400 interactions per SME customer in year one, this approach costs £44 per customer annually in activation inference alone. Option A costs £16. The additional £28 per customer — £392K across the SME activation base — funds inference on sessions where nothing has changed in the customer's context and the guidance adds no marginal value.
options.insightRevenue: The guidance quality is not in question. The timing is. A customer who dismisses guidance prompts after two weeks of irrelevant suggestions activates fewer features — not because the AI was unhelpful, but because the signal-to-noise ratio eroded the utility of the channel. The CVI trajectory shows early strength that weakens as prompt fatigue sets in.

compareSummary.reason: Produces better guidance quality than scheduled updates — but spends £900K more than Option A to run inference on sessions where the customer's context hasn't changed and the guidance adds no marginal value.

options.explanation: The highest-capability model at every session is a technology preference applied without cost discipline. The inference cost of £0.11 per interaction is 2.75x Option A. The quality difference per interaction is marginal for routine sessions — a customer checking their balance does not benefit from a reasoning model generating fresh contextual guidance. The cost difference is not marginal: across 140,000 activation interactions per year, the model choice adds £900K in inference cost for guidance that frequently arrives when the customer's context hasn't changed. The compounding consequence: £900K unavailable at Engagement, where the same budget funds a CFO agent that catches Aisha's cash flow crisis before she knows it exists. Prompt fatigue compounds the investment: customers who dismiss irrelevant guidance don't stop dismissing it when it becomes relevant.

options.label: The system generates an activation guide for Aisha at account opening, then sends scheduled updates every 48 hours based on her account state — regardless of whether she's actively configuring anything. Predictable inference cost, predictable delivery cadence. Cost: £350K. Cost per interaction: £0.025.
options.insightExperience: Aisha received an activation guide on day one — accurate, helpful, well-written. The follow-up update arrived 48 hours later, while she was in service on a Saturday evening. The FX guidance arrived on a Tuesday morning when she wasn't thinking about supplier payments. By the time she set up her euro payment schedule, she had already navigated the process herself — the guidance arrived three days after she'd needed it.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £0.025 per interaction, this is the cheapest activation approach. The cost saving versus Option A is £350K. The commercial consequence is a structural timing mismatch: guidance is generated on a schedule, not in response to customer behaviour. The £350K saved does not compensate for the feature adoption gap created by guidance that arrives at the wrong moment.
options.insightRevenue: Aisha configured payroll correctly. She never set up the FX alert for her supplier payments — the guidance arrived when she wasn't in that context, and she moved on. She discovered six months later that she had been paying the bank's default FX spread on every euro invoice rather than the competitive rate she could have locked. The missed feature activation compounds: lower FX revenue for the bank, lower satisfaction for Aisha, a support call that could have been an upsell.

compareSummary.reason: Saves £350K versus Option A but creates a structural timing mismatch — guidance arrives on a schedule, not when Aisha's context signals she needs it. The most critical activation features go unconfigured because the guidance missed the moment.

options.explanation: Scheduled guidance optimises for cost, not for impact. A 48-hour update cycle is independent of what Aisha is actually doing: it delivers guidance when it is convenient for the system, not when it is relevant to the customer. The AIX framework's Intent Alignment dimension is clear: the AI must surface outcomes that serve what the user is actually trying to accomplish at that moment. A scheduled update cannot do this — it can only approximate it by generating broadly relevant content on a fixed cadence. The consequence is structural: the highest-value features (FX management, cash flow alerts tied to payroll) require guidance at the exact moment of first use. Miss that moment and the feature goes unconfigured. An unconfigured FX alert is not just a missed upsell — it is a missed protection for Aisha's cash flow, the very problem she told you about when you interviewed her.

rounds.title: It's October. Aisha has £18K in unpaid invoices and payroll in 8 days. She doesn't know yet.
rounds.tradeoffTagline: 🤖 CFO agent scope vs 🔒 Data permissions vs ⏰ Timing
rounds.prompt: Aisha is three months into her relationship with the bank. Her Hackney expansion plans are in early research. Right now, in October, she has a cash flow problem forming that she hasn't noticed yet: three invoices are overdue, her main food supplier has increased prices by 12%, and payroll for 12 employees is due in 8 days. Her account balance looks fine today. It will not look fine in 6 days. The bank must decide what kind of AI intelligence it has built — and whether it can see this coming.

options.label: The bank builds a CFO agent with full external data integration — connecting Aisha's bank account to her invoicing software (Xero), her suppliers' payment portals, and her HMRC VAT schedule. Maximum context, maximum intelligence. But Aisha must grant permissions for each data source. Approximately 35% of SMEs decline at least one permission. Cost: £1.4M. Cost per alert: £0.18.
options.insightExperience: For the 65% of SME customers who granted all permissions: the CFO agent caught the October cash flow gap 6 days in advance and surfaced a working capital facility. For the 35% who declined one or more permissions: the agent ran on incomplete data and missed the gap. Aisha was in the 65% — but the bank built an expensive, fragile system dependent on customer permissions it cannot guarantee.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £1.4M, this is £500K more than Option B — and 35% of that investment delivers Option B quality at best, because the external data pipelines only work when customers grant permissions. The per-alert cost of £0.18 is also the highest in this round: external data retrieval adds inference cost at every alert event.
options.insightRevenue: For the cohort that granted permissions, the revenue outcome approaches Option B. For the 35% who didn't, it falls toward Option C. The aggregate outcome is a blend — better than reactive monitoring, but below what internal-only intelligence can deliver when designed correctly.

compareSummary.reason: The ceiling is higher than Option B — but it is dependent on permissions that 35% of SMEs will not grant. The floor is Option C. You pay for Option A and frequently get Option B or below.

options.explanation: Full external integration is the right destination — but the wrong first step. The system's effectiveness depends on a permission layer that approximately 35% of SME customers will not complete. Privacy-cautious business owners, customers suspicious of data sharing, and SMEs with complex multi-entity structures like Aisha's all present permission friction. The bank built a sophisticated, expensive intelligence system and made it contingent on customer behaviour it cannot control. The three-layer framework is explicit: architecture decisions must sustain margin without eroding it. A £1.4M system that delivers full capability to 65% of customers is a more complex, more expensive version of Option B. Build the internal engine correctly first. Add external data integration in Phase 2, when the internal intelligence has proven its value and customers have a reason to trust the permission request.

options.label: The bank builds a CFO agent on internal data only — monitoring Aisha's account balances, transaction history, payroll schedule, and payment patterns. No external data connections required. No permissions needed. The agent catches the October gap 6 days early and surfaces a working capital facility. Cost: £900K. Cost per alert: £0.15.
options.insightExperience: Six days before her cash flow crisis, Aisha received an in-app notification: 'Based on your payroll schedule and current outstanding invoices, your account will be £6,200 below your payroll requirement by 28 October. We have a working capital facility available — would you like to review it?' She hadn't noticed. The bank had. That moment — a specific prediction, a specific number, an actionable offer — is the experience that changes the relationship from transactional to trusted.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £900K and £0.15 per alert, the internal CFO agent is £500K less than external integration and requires no permission layer. The bank's internal data — transaction history, payroll schedule, payment cadences — is sufficient to detect the October gap. It cannot model Aisha's invoice aging in Xero — but it can see which payments haven't cleared and when payroll is due. That is enough to catch the crisis.
options.insightRevenue: A cash flow crisis caught 6 days early — before Aisha knows it exists — is worth £3.5M in retained lifetime value across the SME base. A working capital facility activated at the right moment generates direct lending revenue. The trust compound from a proactive intervention at a genuine moment of financial risk is the highest single CEI uplift available at this stage.

compareSummary.reason: Delivers the highest revenue outcome at the lowest cost — internal data is sufficient to catch the crisis, and the absence of a permission layer means the capability works for 100% of the SME base, not 65%.

options.explanation: This is the correct decision — and it applies the most important sequencing principle in AI product development: build the simplest system that works correctly before building the most sophisticated system that works conditionally. The bank's internal data — account balances, transaction history, direct debit schedules, payroll patterns — is sufficient to detect Aisha's October cash flow gap. It cannot see her Xero invoice aging or her supplier's payment portal. But it can see that three expected inflows have not arrived, that payroll is in 8 days, and that her current balance less those payroll debits equals a shortfall. That is the inference. At £0.15 per alert, the cost is justified by the revenue outcome: a working capital facility activated at the right moment, a trust event that compounds through Retention and Loyalty, and a customer who now believes the bank is genuinely watching her interests. Build the external data layer next. First, prove the internal intelligence.

options.label: The bank uses AI to generate a monthly cash flow summary report for each SME customer. A relationship manager reviews the highest-risk accounts and calls where necessary. The October gap is flagged in Aisha's November report. Cost: £500K. Cost per report: £0.06.
options.insightExperience: Aisha's October cash flow crisis was flagged in the November monthly report. By then, she had already called her accountant in a panic, negotiated an informal overdraft arrangement, and delayed a supplier payment by 12 days — damaging a key relationship. The bank's AI correctly identified the risk — one month after the window for effective action had closed.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £0.06 per report, this is the cheapest engagement approach. The cost saving versus Option B is £400K annually. The commercial cost of the timing failure is not captured in the inference cost: it is captured in the support call Aisha made during the crisis, the relationship manager time required to remediate, and the trust deficit created by a bank that watches its customers' financial health retrospectively.
options.insightRevenue: Early intervention consistently outperforms late recovery. A cash flow crisis caught 6 days before payroll is a working capital facility conversation. The same crisis identified after the fact is a remediation conversation — and a customer who is evaluating whether the bank is actually watching out for them.

compareSummary.reason: Saves £400K versus Option B but delivers a retrospective system at the stage where proactive intelligence has the highest leverage. The October report arrived in November. The crisis happened in October.

options.explanation: Monthly reporting creates a reactive system at the stage where AI adds the most economic value. The technology is not the problem — the AI correctly identified Aisha's October cash flow risk. The timing is the problem: a batch process that runs on a calendar schedule cannot respond to emerging risk in real time. By the time the November report flags October's gap, Aisha has already navigated the crisis herself — or failed to. The opportunity to intervene proactively — to surface a specific number, a specific date, a specific offer, at the exact moment it would change her behaviour — is the highest-value AI capability the bank can deploy in the SME relationship. Monthly reporting produces accurate retrospectives. The CFO agent produces interventions. These are not the same product.

rounds.title: Aisha asks: 'Should I open my second restaurant in Hackney?' What grounds the answer?
rounds.tradeoffTagline: 🏗️ Build vs 🔌 Buy vs 📡 Retrieve — the recommendation grounding problem
rounds.prompt: Aisha is ready to expand. She has identified Hackney as a potential location for her second restaurant — strong local food scene, growing residential density, a property available at a competitive rent. She asks the bank's AI: 'Can I afford this, and is Hackney the right location?' The bank must decide what grounds the recommendation: a proprietary model trained on its own SME transaction data, a third-party specialist analytics platform, or a retrieval system that pulls live signals in real time.

options.label: The bank builds a proprietary AI model trained on its 50,000 SME transaction histories — including 3,200 restaurant businesses. High accuracy for patterns the model has seen before. Aisha's Middle Eastern artisan restaurant concept doesn't match the restaurant archetypes in the training data. The model recommends Hackney with moderate confidence. Cost to build: £1.9M. Cost per query: £0.12.
options.insightExperience: The model recommended Hackney with moderate confidence. The recommendation was grounded in patterns from existing restaurant customers — Italian, Indian, and American casual dining formats that make up the majority of the bank's restaurant data. Aisha's Middle Eastern artisan concept performed differently than the model expected. The model's confidence was not calibrated to her category.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £1.9M to build and £0.12 per query, this is the most expensive approach in this round. The training cost funds proprietary capability — but the proprietary capability is only as good as the training data. The training data is a historical record of the bank's existing customers, which skews toward conventional restaurant formats. The model's accuracy for conventional patterns is high. Its accuracy for Aisha is lower than its confidence score suggests.
options.insightRevenue: Initial conversion is strong — the recommendation feels specific and bank-backed. Trust erodes when Aisha notices the model's limitations: it recommended a location based on performance data from restaurants unlike hers, and its projections didn't account for the specific demand dynamics of her cuisine category. The late-stage trajectory deteriorates as the recommendation gap becomes apparent.

compareSummary.reason: Costs £700K more than Option C and produces lower accuracy for atypical SME categories — the proprietary model is a historical record of the bank's existing customers, not a live signal of the market Aisha is entering.

options.explanation: A proprietary model creates a structural accuracy problem: it learns from what the bank already knows, not from what Aisha needs to understand. The bank's 3,200 restaurant customers are predominantly conventional formats — Italian, Indian, American casual dining. The model has excellent accuracy for those archetypes. For an artisan Middle Eastern restaurant concept expanding into Hackney's specific micro-market, the model applies patterns from dissimilar businesses. It recommends Hackney — correctly, as it happens — but for the wrong reasons and with miscalibrated confidence. When Hackney's early trading differs from the model's projections, Aisha questions the bank's intelligence. Trust in the AI's recommendations falls. The £1.9M build cost funds a model that will become progressively less accurate as the market evolves and the training data ages.

options.label: The bank integrates with a specialist restaurant analytics platform — deep sector data, category-specific performance benchmarks, foot traffic analysis, and competitor mapping. Best specificity for Aisha's use case. Requires a data sharing agreement: Aisha's financial data is shared with the vendor. Vendor charges per query. Cost: £800K integration + £0.15 per query. Vendor contract: 3-year lock-in.
options.insightExperience: The recommendation was highly specific — category benchmarks for Middle Eastern cuisine in East London, foot traffic patterns for the Hackney micro-market, rent-to-revenue ratios for comparable restaurant formats. Aisha was impressed by the specificity. She later discovered that her financial data had been shared with the analytics vendor without her being clearly informed. That discovery eroded trust.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £0.15 per query — the highest per-query cost in this round — and a 3-year vendor contract, the bank has created a fixed cost architecture that cannot be renegotiated based on performance. The integration cost of £800K is lower than building proprietary capability, but the ongoing query cost and vendor dependency accumulate over the contract term.
options.insightRevenue: Initial recommendation quality is high. The vendor lock-in and data sharing consequences emerge later: when the contract comes up for renewal, the vendor is in a strong negotiating position. When Aisha learns her data left the bank's perimeter, her willingness to share additional data — and to trust the bank's AI recommendations — weakens.

compareSummary.reason: Better category specificity than Option A for Aisha's use case — but the vendor lock-in, data sharing requirement, and highest per-query cost in the round create dependencies that weaken the bank's position over time.

options.explanation: The recommendation quality is genuinely superior for Aisha's specific category — this is the advantage of specialist analytics over a general-purpose proprietary model. But the commercial architecture creates three compounding problems. First, data sharing: Aisha's financial data leaves the bank's perimeter without clear customer disclosure, creating a trust and regulatory exposure. Second, vendor lock-in: three years of fixed commercial terms with a specialist vendor eliminates the bank's flexibility to switch to better technology as the market evolves. Third, per-query cost: at £0.15 per query — 2.5x Option C — the unit economics deteriorate as recommendation volume grows. The bank paid for intelligence that is accurate today and creates dependencies it will pay for for three years.

options.label: The bank builds a retrieval-augmented generation system — the AI pulls live signals at query time: Companies House filings for new restaurant registrations in Hackney, property transaction data for commercial rents, sector delivery platform performance data, and the bank's own SME cash flow benchmarks. No proprietary model training. No vendor data sharing. No per-query vendor charge. Cost: £1.2M. Cost per query: £0.06.
options.insightExperience: The AI retrieved live data at query time and responded: 'Hackney is a strong second location. In the past 18 months, 14 new restaurants have opened in the target area — 4 in your cuisine category, with an average break-even of 16 months. Commercial rents on your target street have increased 8% year-on-year. Your cash flow profile versus comparable SMEs at this stage suggests you could support a £120K–£150K expansion loan with manageable debt service.' The recommendation was grounded in live signals, not historical archetypes. Aisha could see exactly what the AI had retrieved and why.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £0.06 per query — less than half the vendor cost and 50% of the proprietary model cost — RAG is the most cost-efficient option. No training data to age, no vendor contract to renew, no data to share outside the bank's perimeter. The retrieval layer is updated automatically as underlying data sources update. The system's accuracy improves as the market evolves, not despite it.
options.insightRevenue: Recommendations grounded in live signals and visible reasoning convert at higher rates — because Aisha can verify the logic, not just trust the output. The trust compound from transparent, accurate, actionable expansion intelligence carries through Loyalty. The Hackney loan generates direct lending revenue. The recommendation quality drives advocacy: Aisha refers two other restaurant owners to the bank within 12 months.

compareSummary.reason: Delivers better recommendation accuracy than proprietary model training at £700K less cost, with no vendor dependency, no data sharing, and per-query cost that is less than half the vendor rate.

options.explanation: This is the correct decision — and it reflects the architecture principle at the heart of the LLM Economics Decision Framework: the intelligence quality of a recommendation comes from the relevance of the grounding data, not from the sophistication of the training process. A retrieval-augmented system that pulls live Companies House data, real-time property transactions, and delivery platform performance has better accuracy for Aisha's specific query than a proprietary model trained on historical data from similar-but-not-identical businesses. At £0.06 per query, it costs less. It creates no vendor dependency. Aisha's data stays within the bank's perimeter. The reasoning is visible and verifiable — which satisfies the AIX Trust dimension: the experience must be reliable, explainable, and safe, especially for high-stakes financial decisions. Aisha can see exactly what the AI retrieved and why it made the recommendation. That transparency is not a UX feature — it is the mechanism of trust at the highest-stakes decision in her banking journey.

rounds.title: Aisha's Hackney branch is underperforming. The AI has flagged her as at-risk. What happens next?
rounds.tradeoffTagline: 🤖 Autonomous action vs 🧠 Human accountability vs ⏳ Reactive timing
rounds.prompt: Fourteen months into the relationship, Aisha's Hackney restaurant is in its early growth phase — trading below initial projections. Her transaction volume at the bank has dropped 18%. She has had two conversations with a competitor's relationship manager. The bank's AI has flagged her as a retention risk. What it does next will determine whether this is a trust-building event or the beginning of the end of the relationship.

options.label: The bank waits for Aisha to raise a concern or show explicit churn signals — a closure request or a direct statement of intent to switch — before responding. No proactive outreach. Minimal cost. Cost: £100K. Cost per intervention: £0.00 (no proactive intervention made).
options.insightExperience: Aisha opened an account with the competitor bank in month 17. She didn't tell her original bank she was considering it. There were no explicit churn signals until the direct debit schedules started moving. By then, the conversation was remedial — not relational.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £100K, this is the cheapest retention approach by far. The cost of not intervening is not in the AI spend — it is in the lost lifetime value of a two-restaurant SME customer at peak CLV. A customer who leaves at this stage takes with them the lending relationship, the FX revenue, the working capital facility, and the referral network she has built. The cost of inaction is not £100K. It is the full CLV of the relationship from month 17 onward.
options.insightRevenue: Early intervention consistently outperforms late recovery at retention. The bank detected the risk 3 months before Aisha left. It acted on that detection zero times. The intervention window was open for 12 weeks and never used.

compareSummary.reason: Saves £900K in retention AI spend, then loses the full remaining CLV of a two-restaurant SME at peak value. The timing failure is the most commercially consequential decision in the simulation.

options.explanation: Waiting for explicit churn signals means the intervention arrives after the relationship has already been psychologically vacated. Aisha started conversations with a competitor bank 14 months into her relationship — triggered by a combination of Hackney underperformance anxiety and a competitor who made the first move. The bank had a 3-month window — visible in the transaction volume decline, the support contact frequency, and the changed payment patterns — during which a proactive, transparent conversation could have been the difference. The AI detected the risk. No architecture was built to act on it. The cost of detection without action is higher than the cost of not detecting: the bank knew, and chose not to respond.

options.label: The AI acts autonomously on Aisha's risk signals — increases her credit facility by £15K, reduces her monthly account fee by 30%, and sends a push notification: 'We've updated your account terms to support your Hackney growth phase.' No human approval. No explanation of what triggered the changes. Cost: £1.4M. Cost per intervention: £0.19.
options.insightExperience: Aisha logged into her account to find her credit limit had been increased and her fee reduced. She hadn't asked for either. The notification gave no explanation of what had changed or why. At a moment of financial uncertainty about Hackney, discovering that the bank had made changes to her account without asking — even generous ones — felt controlling rather than supportive.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £1.4M and £0.19 per intervention, this is the most expensive retention approach. The spending is on autonomous action — continuous risk monitoring, signal classification, and automated intervention execution — without any of the governance infrastructure that would make the action trustworthy. Cost is high. Trust outcome is negative.
options.insightRevenue: Retention metrics improve in the short term — Aisha doesn't immediately leave. But the trust damage from unexplained autonomous action on her financial account at a moment of vulnerability creates a Loyalty-stage collapse. She stayed. She didn't deepen the relationship. She started looking for alternatives within 6 months.

compareSummary.reason: Prevents the immediate churn that Option C triggers — but the autonomous, unexplained action on Aisha's account at a financially sensitive moment creates a trust deficit that compounds through Loyalty.

options.explanation: Acting without explanation on someone's financial account — at the moment they are most anxious about their financial position — is the most consequential trust violation an AI can commit in financial services. The AI's intent was correct: Aisha needed support, the credit facility increase and fee reduction were the right gestures. The execution was wrong: no human reviewed the decision, no explanation was provided to Aisha, and the changes appeared in her account without her participation. The AIX Agency & Control dimension is explicit: Aisha must be the decision-maker, not just the recipient of automated generosity. The AI must operate within visible, understandable boundaries. When an SME discovers that her bank's AI modified her account terms without asking — even to her benefit — the question that follows is: what else can it change without asking? That question, once asked, does not have a satisfactory answer.

options.label: The AI detects the risk signals, flags them for a relationship manager with a specific brief, and the relationship manager calls Aisha within 24 hours. The call opens: 'We've noticed Hackney is in its early growth phase and your transaction patterns have shifted — we wanted to check in and see how we can support you.' Aisha is told exactly what the bank saw and what it proposes. Cost: £1.0M. Cost per intervention: £0.14.
options.insightExperience: The relationship manager called on a Tuesday morning. She opened with specific information — Hackney, transaction patterns, the shift the bank had noticed — and offered a structured review of Aisha's working capital position. Aisha hadn't known the bank was watching so closely. The fact that it was, and that it called before she reached out, changed her perception of the relationship fundamentally.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £1.0M and £0.14 per intervention — £400K less than autonomous action — the human-approved model is cheaper and produces better outcomes. The AI does the detection and briefing; the human does the intervention. The cost of the relationship manager call is absorbed by the retention outcome: a retained two-restaurant SME at peak CLV generates materially more revenue over the subsequent 36 months than the intervention cost.
options.insightRevenue: Aisha did not switch banks. She deepened the relationship: she expanded her FX facility, took the working capital top-up, and referred two restaurant owner contacts within 6 months. The CEI uplift at Retention — when intervention is transparent and human-approved — is the highest in the simulation. Retained trust at this stage is compounding equity.

compareSummary.reason: At £400K less than autonomous action, it delivers five times the revenue — the human review step turns the intervention from a trust risk into a trust-building event, and that difference is the entire outcome gap.

options.explanation: This is the correct decision — and it reflects the most important governance principle in the LLM Economics Decision Framework: autonomy drives scale and speed, but increases risk; human oversight adds control but reduces efficiency, and the balance is critical. At a stage where Aisha is financially anxious and already evaluating competitors, autonomous action on her account — even generous action — violates the Agency & Control dimension of AIX. The human-approved model preserves that dimension: the AI detects, briefs, and prepares; the human decides and communicates. The customer is told exactly what was observed and exactly what is being proposed. She participates in the decision. That participation is the mechanism of trust — and trust retained at Retention is the highest-CLV asset on the bank's SME book.

rounds.title: Aisha's second restaurant is profitable. A brand wants to license her concept. How does the bank's AI shape this moment?
rounds.tradeoffTagline: 🌱 Long-term partnership vs 💵 Commercial extraction vs 🎲 Co-investment risk
rounds.prompt: Twenty months into the relationship. Hackney is trading profitably. Aisha now employs 24 people across two sites. A regional food brand has approached her about licensing her restaurant concept — a potential franchise opportunity. She is at the peak of her SME banking value: two properties, a strong lending relationship, growing FX volume, and a referral network of 6 business owners she has already introduced to the bank. The bank must decide what its AI does at this moment.

options.label: The bank uses its AI to model Aisha's licensing opportunity — evaluating the franchise structure, the capital requirement, and the risk profile — and proactively proposes to co-invest in the franchise expansion alongside her as a commercial partner. A specialist franchise finance product. High ceiling if Aisha accepts. New risk category for the bank. Cost: £600K AI + significant commercial team resource.
options.insightExperience: Aisha was surprised to receive a co-investment proposal from the bank — she hadn't asked for one. The proposal was detailed and well-modelled. But it changed the nature of the conversation: suddenly the bank was not her financial partner, it was a potential co-owner of her concept. That change in relationship dynamic — unsolicited — introduced a complexity she wasn't ready for.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £600K in AI modelling cost plus commercial team resource for structuring a novel franchise finance product, the bank is investing in a capability it doesn't currently have for a customer who didn't ask for it. The highest-ceiling outcomes require Aisha to say yes to a relationship change she may not want at this stage of her business.
options.insightRevenue: The proposal generates significant analysis and commercial team cost. If Aisha accepts, the upside is substantial. If she declines — which is more likely when an unsolicited co-investment proposal arrives at a moment of growth — the bank has invested in an offer that complicated the relationship and generated no revenue.

compareSummary.reason: Bold, well-intentioned — but the co-investment proposal introduces a relationship dynamic Aisha didn't request at the moment she most values the bank's intelligence, not its commercial ambitions.

options.explanation: The co-investment proposal is the right idea at the wrong time, delivered in the wrong way. Aisha is at peak CLV and high trust — this is exactly the moment where the bank's AI should be demonstrating its value as an intelligence partner. Instead, it proposes to become a commercial partner — an unsolicited shift in the nature of the relationship that Aisha must now evaluate, negotiate, and potentially decline. The AIX Agency & Control dimension is violated: the customer should decide whether to expand the relationship into new territory; the bank's AI should enable that decision, not make it for her. A co-investment conversation initiated by Aisha — after the AI has given her the intelligence to evaluate the licensing opportunity — is a very different conversation from one initiated by the bank as a surprise proposal.

options.label: The AI identifies cross-sell opportunities based on Aisha's business profile and surfaces them in order of bank margin: business insurance, FX hedging, a premium account tier, pension auto-enrolment. Each product is genuinely useful for a growing two-restaurant SME. The AI surfaces them because they are margin-positive for the bank. Cost: £1.0M. Cost per recommendation: £0.12.
options.insightExperience: The products the AI surfaced were all relevant to Aisha's business. The order in which they were surfaced — premium account tier first, then FX hedging, then insurance — reflected bank margin, not Aisha's priorities. She noticed. Not consciously at first. But the recommendations felt increasingly promotional over three months, and she started dismissing them without reading.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £1.0M and £0.12 per recommendation, this is more expensive than Option A. The products convert at reasonable rates — they are genuinely useful. But the recommendation ordering, driven by commercial priority rather than customer need, erodes the signal value of the channel over time. Customers who stop engaging with recommendations cost the bank more per conversion in future.
options.insightRevenue: Short-term cross-sell revenue is real. The trust erosion is slower but compounding: a customer who begins to interpret AI recommendations as promotional rather than advisory reduces her engagement with the recommendation layer, increases her receptiveness to competitive outreach, and generates lower referral value. Advocacy is the highest-CLV output of the Loyalty stage — and extraction-oriented AI does not generate it.

compareSummary.reason: Generates more short-term cross-sell revenue than Option C — but the recommendation ordering by margin erodes the channel's signal value and the customer's trust in a way that reduces lifetime value faster than the cross-sell revenue grows it.

options.explanation: The products are not wrong. The objective function is. An AI that surfaces products in order of bank margin is not optimising for customer outcomes — it is optimising for short-term revenue at the expense of long-term trust. Aisha has been a bank customer for 20 months. She has been through a cash flow crisis that the bank caught, a retention risk that the bank handled with transparency, and an expansion decision that the bank grounded in live market intelligence. She now has a calibrated sense of what 'this bank's AI genuinely serves my interests' feels like. When the recommendations shift from intelligence to promotion — even subtly, even with genuinely useful products — she will notice. The trust that has been built over 20 months and 6 major decisions is the most valuable asset on the bank's SME book. An extraction-oriented AI at Loyalty trades that asset for margin on an insurance product.

options.label: The AI surfaces intelligence that serves Aisha's growth: an analysis of the franchise licensing opportunity, cash flow modelling for a third location, sector benchmarks comparing her performance against similar businesses at the same stage. The bank's revenue is the downstream consequence of being the intelligence partner Aisha trusts at her most consequential decisions. Cost: £800K. Cost per insight: £0.10.
options.insightExperience: The AI surfaced a franchise licensing analysis Aisha hadn't asked for — but immediately recognised as exactly what she needed. The analysis showed the capital structure of comparable restaurant franchise models, the cash flow implications of the licensing fee structure, and a comparison of her current financial position against businesses that had made the same decision. The bank's intelligence was serving her goals, not its own.
options.insightCostDrivers: At £800K and £0.10 per insight — the lowest cost in this round — serving customer outcomes costs less than extraction. The intelligence the AI provides draws on the retrieval infrastructure built at Expansion and the CFO agent built at Engagement. No new capability required. The insight is generated from assets the bank has already built, deployed at the moment they generate the highest value.
options.insightRevenue: Aisha used the franchise analysis to negotiate her licensing terms. She referred three additional restaurant owners to the bank within the following year — specifically citing the bank's intelligence as the reason. Each referral generates a new SME relationship at zero acquisition cost. The compounding CLV of a loyal, advocacy-generating SME at peak value — banking revenue, lending revenue, FX revenue, referrals — is the highest return the simulation can produce.

compareSummary.reason: At £200K less than Option B, it generates more than three times the revenue — because the intelligence serves Aisha's growth rather than the bank's margin, and advocacy is worth more than cross-sell conversion.

options.explanation: This is the correct decision — and it closes the argument that has run across all seven stages of the simulation. The LLM Economics Decision Framework is explicit: experience decisions, architecture decisions, and commercial decisions must be made together, not sequentially. At Loyalty, the experience decision is clear: serve Aisha's growth. The architecture decision follows: deploy the intelligence infrastructure already built — the retrieval layer from Expansion, the CFO agent from Engagement — to generate insights about the franchise opportunity she is evaluating. The commercial decision is downstream: the bank's revenue is the consequence of being the intelligence partner that Aisha trusts at her most consequential decisions, not the product she is being sold to this month. Serving customer outcomes costs less and earns more than extraction. The compounding value of trust — built correctly at every stage from Onboarding through Loyalty — is the asset. The AI's job at Loyalty is not to monetise that asset. It is to compound it.
